stem: When teaching a transplant candidate about transplantation risks, which outcome should the coordinator include as part of standard risk disclosure?

options.text: Rejection can occur at any time after implantation of the organ
Rejection occurs only during the first 24 hours after surgery
Rejection never occurs once immunosuppression is started
Rejection is limited to pediatric recipients only

explanation.rationale_correct: Risk teaching includes organ rejection, which can occur at any time after implantation of the organ(s) when the immune system recognizes the transplant as foreign.

rationale_incorrect.B: Rejection is not confined to the immediate perioperative period; it may occur at any time after implantation.
rationale_incorrect.C: Immunosuppression reduces rejection risk but does not eliminate the possibility of rejection at any time.
rationale_incorrect.D: Rejection risk applies to solid-organ recipients broadly, not pediatric recipients alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → 6. Risks associated with transplantation → b. Organ rejection → ii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Rejection can occur at any time after implantation of the organ(s)

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → 6. Risks associated with transplantation → b. Organ rejection → ii. (rejection can occur at any time after implantation); PDF p. 98 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Seventh 010100 item; general/both-age rejection-risk angle distinct from waitlist mortality (cctc-1022) and smoking risks (cctc-1034); anchor verified on Cupples p. 98.

stem: Before discharge, a recipient is started on insulin for post-transplant hyperglycemia. Which teaching element should the coordinator verify per standard discharge education references?

options.text: Patient and caregiver can demonstrate correct insulin preparation and administration with site rotation
Insulin may be stopped permanently once the patient leaves the hospital
Glucometer use is optional and never requires return demonstration
Hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia symptoms require no team contact parameters

explanation.rationale_correct: Discharge diabetic education includes insulin administration teaching with return demonstration of drawing up or dialing the correct dosage, preparing the injection site, and rotating sites.

rationale_incorrect.B: Insulin and glucose management continue after discharge under team guidance rather than being stopped at hospital discharge.
rationale_incorrect.C: Patients and caregivers should demonstrate glucometer use and insulin technique when insulin is prescribed.
rationale_incorrect.D: Teaching includes signs and symptoms of hypo- and hyperglycemia and parameters for contacting the team managing glucose control.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → B. Diabetic education → insulin administration
primary_anchor.quote_hint: return demonstration including drawing up or dialing up the correct dosage … rotation of sites

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → B. Diabetic education (glucometer demonstration; insulin administration return demonstration and site rotation); PDF p. 112 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Eleventh 010500 item; discharge insulin-teaching angle distinct from medication complex_combo (cctc-1033) and osteopenia (cctc-1047); anchor verified on Cupples p. 112.

stem: A coordinator is reviewing transplantation risk teaching with a candidate and family. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Death may occur on the waiting list, during transplant surgery, or after transplantation.
Rejection can occur at any time after organ implantation.
Lifetime immunosuppression is never required after solid-organ transplant.
Primary nonfunction may require immediate relisting and retransplantation.

explanation.rationale_correct: Standard risk teaching includes death on the waitlist, during surgery, or after transplant; rejection at any time after implantation; need for lifetime immunosuppression; and primary nonfunction that may require immediate relisting.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also correct—primary nonfunction may require immediate relisting.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statements I and II are also true; statement III is false because lifetime immunosuppression is required.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false; lifetime immunosuppression is a recognized transplant requirement.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → 6. Risks associated with transplantation
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Death … On the waiting list … Organ rejection … any time … Need for lifetime immunosuppression … Primary nonfunction may require immediate relisting

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → 6. Risks associated with transplantation (death, rejection, lifetime immunosuppression, primary nonfunction); PDF p. 98 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Synthesized item. Thirteenth complex_combo in bank; distinct from infection-prevention (cctc-1024) and dietary (cctc-1052) combos; anchor verified on Cupples p. 98.

stem: When counseling the family of a recently transplanted child about community-acquired infections, which teaching point aligns with standard infection-prevention references?

options.text: Community-acquired infections can be more severe in young children, especially soon after transplant during heavy immunosuppression
Community infections are always mild in children regardless of immunosuppression timing
Pediatric recipients have no risk of influenza or respiratory syncytial virus after transplant
Immunosuppression eliminates the need to evaluate fever in pediatric recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Community-acquired infections can be more severe in young children, especially if they occur soon after transplantation and during highly immunosuppressed periods.

rationale_incorrect.B: Severity risk is heightened in young children during early highly immunosuppressed periods rather than being uniformly mild.
rationale_incorrect.C: Pediatric recipients remain at risk for common childhood illnesses including influenza and respiratory syncytial virus.
rationale_incorrect.D: Fever evaluation remains important; immunosuppression increases rather than eliminates infection concern.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 17, Pediatric Populations → H. Community-acquired infections → 1.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Community-acquired infections can be more severe in young children, especially if they occur soon after transplantation

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 17 → H. Community-acquired infections → 1. (more severe in young children soon after transplant during heavy immunosuppression); PDF p. 944 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Twelfth 010600 item; fifth pediatric recipient in bank; community-infection angle distinct from HPV (cctc-1036) and live-virus household (cctc-1046); anchor verified on Cupples p. 944.
